extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computational number theorists using the Magma computer algebra system
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reference for using Magma functions and algorithms related to number fields: ideals, unit groups, class groups, quadratic forms, and real/complex (approximate) fields. Describes available intrinsics, their meanings, computational behaviour, and important algorithmic/tradeoff notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal representations in orders
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal in an order can be represented either by a ZZ-basis (integral basis) or by a two-element representation; any ideal in an order can be generated by at most two elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Basis(I) to obtain a ZZ-basis (returns matrix rows showing basis vectors). Use Generators(I) to return two elements in the order, and TwoElement(I) to return two elements in the field that generate I; TwoElementNormal provides a more sophisticated two-element presentation. Two-element representations may be more expensive to compute initially but are often cheaper to use afterwards. Example outputs are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal arithmetic and principal multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideals may be multiplied, exponentiated, or multiplied by an order element (equivalent to multiplication by the principal ideal generated by that element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use normal algebraic operators (product, power) on ideals. Multiplication by an order element corresponds to multiplying by the principal ideal generated by that element. Examples demonstrate checking equality (J^2 eq I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime factor decomposition of ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: The prime ideal factorization of an ideal is returned by Factorization(I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factorization(I) returns the factorization into prime ideals and their exponents; elements of the Factorization output can be indexed to extract component ideals. Use Decomposition(O, p) to factor the (integral) ideal p*O for a rational prime p (gives prime ideals of O dividing p and their exponents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractional ideals representation and denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: Division of ideals can produce fractional ideals, represented similarly to integral ideals but with an integral denominator d such that d·J is integral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fractional ideals print with two-element generators and a denominator. Use inverse J^-1 to obtain fractional ideal; denominators indicate minimal integer clearing factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: IsPrincipal predicate and generator return
rubrics_metrics.description: IsPrincipal(I) returns true if a fractional ideal I is generated by a single element; if true, it also returns such a generator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test may be time-consuming in large orders. Example: IsPrincipal(J) returned true and a generator (printed). Use with caution on large orders due to computational cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal-related predicates and auxiliary functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Various predicates and functions test or return properties related to ideals: IsZero, IsIntegral, IsPrime, Valuation, MultiplicatorRing, pRadical, DegreeOnePrimeIdeals, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table lists meanings: IsZero(I) true if zero ideal; IsIntegral(I) true if integral; IsPrime(I) true if prime; Valuation(I,J) gives valuation of I at prime J; MultiplicatorRing(I) returns subring of elements multiplying I into itself; pRadical(O,p) returns ideal of elements with some power in pO. Use DegreeOnePrimeIdeals(O,b) to list degree-1 prime ideals up to norm b. Multiplicator ring and p-radical are used in maximal order algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class group / class number functions
rubrics_metrics.description: ClassNumber(K), ClassGroup(K), and ClassGroupStructure(K) provide respectively the class number, the class group (with mapping to ideals), and invariants/structure of the class group for the ring of integers of K (maximal order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ClassGroup returns two values: an abstract abelian group A and a homomorphism mapping A to its realization (ideals). ClassNumber gives just the cardinality; ClassGroupStructure gives the abelian invariants. For orders, ClassGroup may only be applied if the order is known to be maximal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit group functions and separation of abstract vs realization
rubrics_metrics.description: UnitGroup(K) (and related functions) return both an abstract abelian group describing the unit group and a homomorphism mapping that abstract group to actual elements (units) in the field or order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UnitGroup returns two values: an abelian group A (in GrpAb) describing torsion+free part and a mapping to the realization inside the field (elements or ideals). This separation lets one inspect abstract structure and actual generators independently (examples shown for Q(i)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit rank determined by signature
rubrics_metrics.description: The free rank (unit rank) of the unit group equals r + s − 1, where r is number of real embeddings and s is number of pairs of complex embeddings (the field signature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the task of computing the unit group reduces to computing torsion (roots of unity) and finding generators for the free part of the predicted rank. UnitRank(K) returns this integer. Use this to anticipate dimension of independent units to find.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of fundamental unit in real quadratic fields
rubrics_metrics.description: FundamentalUnit(K) returns a fundamental unit for a real quadratic field K; the fundamental unit has norm ±1 and may have very large coefficients, making computation difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding a fundamental unit can be computationally intensive; examples show enormous coefficients. Norm constraints (Norm = ±1) connect to Diophantine equations x^2 + d y^2 = ±4. Use NormEquation for solving x^2 + d y^2 = m in imaginary quadratics when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional torsion in quadratic fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Imaginary quadratic fields have torsion = ±1 with two exceptions: Q(i) (4th roots of unity) and Q(sqrt{-3}) (6th roots of unity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UnitGroup applied to these fields returns finite cyclic groups of order 4 or 6 accordingly (example outputs given). Recognize these classical exceptions when interpreting torsion output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary quadratic form representation for quadratic class groups
rubrics_metrics.description: For quadratic fields, the class group can be realized via reduced binary quadratic forms of the field discriminant (one-to-one correspondence for imaginary case, cycles of reduced forms in the real case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ClassGroup for quadratic fields returns mapping from abstract class group to magma of binary quadratic forms. Use QuadraticForms(D) to create magma of forms. Reduction(f) and ReductionStep are provided; Reduction gives unique reduced form in imaginary case, cycles in real case. Table of form operations (Composition, Power, Inverse, Discriminant, PrimeForm, Distance, IsReduced, etc.) is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation method for general class group computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Class groups for general number fields are computed via a relation method: (1) generate factor basis of prime ideals of norm below a bound; (2) find elements whose principal ideals factor over the factor basis to create relations; (3) compute basis for class group and verify orders using unit information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions supporting the method: FactorBasis(K,b), RelationMatrix(K,b,n), MinkowskiBound(K), BachBound(K). To guarantee correctness, include all prime ideals up to Minkowski bound (or Bach bound under GRH). Practical computations often use much smaller bounds for speed, but risk incorrect results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class group computation parameters and correctness tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: ClassNumber, ClassGroupStructure, and ClassGroup implement the full relation method by default using the Minkowski bound, but parameters Bound and Check allow shortcuts at the cost of possibly invalid results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bound can be set smaller than MinkowskiBound to speed up relation-finding; Check := false omits expensive final checks. Warning: too small a bound may omit generators (result too small); omitting checks may miss relations (result too large). Use these parameters only when user accepts potential uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions for obtaining partial or p-fundamental unit information
rubrics_metrics.description: IndependentUnits returns a subgroup of finite index (maximal independent set) of the unit group; pFundamentalUnits returns a subgroup whose index is coprime to p (so pth roots not needed); MergeUnits allows user-supplied units to be incorporated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IndependentUnits may require extracting roots to get true generators. pFundamentalUnits can be much faster and gives subgroup adequate for p-adic considerations. MergeUnits(M,u) adds supplied unit u into stored unit information and returns true if rank increases. Use these to avoid full (expensive) UnitGroup computation when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulator computation triggers unit/maximal order computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulator(O) returns the regulator of an order O and will trigger computation of units (and the maximal order) if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requesting only the regulator can implicitly cause heavier computations; be aware of expensive underlying tasks when calling Regulator.

rubrics_metrics.name: TorsionSubgroup for quick determination of finite part of units
rubrics_metrics.description: TorsionSubgroup(K) usually returns the finite torsion subgroup (roots of unity) quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this when only the finite/unit torsion part is of interest; example shows TorsionSubgroup(M) returning Z/6 with mapping to element. Combine with UnitRank to plan further unit computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real and complex field kinds: free vs fixed precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma has two kinds of real fields: free real fields (each element has its own relative precision, possibly infinite for exact rationals) and fixed-precision real fields (every element has same precision p). Complex fields likewise come as free or fixed-precision (with real and imaginary parts belonging to corresponding real fields).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create fields with RealField() / RealField(p) and ComplexField() / ComplexField(p). Free fields use PARI implementation; fixed-precision fields use MP implementation. Choose based on needs: free for flexible per-element precision and exact rationals; fixed when uniform precision performance is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default real field and precision behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma has a default real field; the free field default has a default precision attribute (28 unless changed). The default determines parent of literals like i.j and behaviour of functions that coerce inputs to reals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GetDefaultRealField() and SetDefaultRealField(R) manage default. HasAttribute(FldPr, "Precision") / AssertAttribute(FldPr, "Precision", new) can inspect/change default precision for the free field; change affects only elements created afterwards. Precision(x) returns relative precision of element; -1 denotes exact (infinite) precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal precision notation and coercion rules (e and p)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific notation with e (i.j e s) creates element in current default real field; appending p with a precision (i.j pN) requests element with specified precision — interpretation depends on whether default is free or fixed-precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If default is free field, p denotes free-field element with requested precision. If default is a fixed-precision field, p denotes request to create an element in a fixed-precision field of that precision. Use elt< RealField(p) | t, s > when exponent/precision are expressions. For fixed fields, precision is rounded up to nearest multiple of 4 (storage base); fixed-precision coercions can truncate irretrievably when reducing precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative precision semantics in free fields and fixed fields
rubrics_metrics.description: In free fields, each element may have its own relative precision (Precision(x)); exact coercions (integers/rationals) have precision -1. In fixed-precision fields all elements share the same precision, and Precision(R) returns that precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coercing elements between precisions: coercing to lower precision can round and lose digits permanently; coercing to higher precision pads with zeros but cannot recover lost information. Fixed-precision interpretation of decimal digits is block-based: precision must account for digits on both sides of decimal point; recommended to set precision ~6 digits higher than desired significant figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coercion and parent dependence for operations returning reals
rubrics_metrics.description: Real-valued functions return values in a real field whose parent depends on the input: if input is from a fixed-precision field, result is in that field; otherwise result belongs to the current default real field after coercion of inputs where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., Parent(Sin(a)) shows parent equals real field of a; Parent(Sin(3/4)) coerces rational to default real field. Be aware that applying real functions to non-real types coerces them into the default real field, triggering default precision rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-precision field storage and digit-block behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed-precision real fields store digits in blocks of 4, rounding requested precision up to a multiple of 4; representation of significant figures depends on blocks on left and right of decimal point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows that to store a number with k significant digits, precision may need to be ~k+6 to account for integer-part digits and internal block alignment. Requests for precision 29–31 become 32, etc. Use elt constructor when precision/exponent are expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex field construction and decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex numbers in Magma are treated as x + i*y with Re(z) and Im(z). Construction via x + i*y (where i is generator assigned when creating the complex field) or F![x,y] coerces x,y into corresponding real fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parent is fixed-precision complex field, real and imaginary parts belong to the corresponding fixed-precision real field; if parent is free complex field, real and imag parts may have different precisions. Use Re(z) and Im(z) to extract parts. Printing examples show slight rounding depending on default/parent fields.
